blocks.text: Paper chromatography is partition chromatography: the water entrapped in the cellulose fibres of the paper and the mobile phase passing over the paper are immiscible, the mobile phase usually being an organic liquid. It is carried out in three ways, ascending, descending and radial (circular); only the ascending type is discussed, in which the solvent travels upwards by capillary action (Figures 15.8 and 15.9).

A solvent mixture composed for the sample is poured into the chromatographic tank, which is covered to homogenise its inner atmosphere. A strip about 20 cm long of Whatman chromatographic paper No. 1 (made from selected cotton cellulose, medium retention and flow rate, pore size 11 micrometres) is marked with a thin pencil line about 2.5 cm from one end, and a spot of the sample mixture solution is placed on the line; spots of known compounds may be placed alongside to help identify the components. When the spots have dried the paper is suspended with clips so that the impregnated end dips 5 to 6 mm into the solvent, and the tank is covered. As the solvent front passes the spots the solutes move upward at different rates, which separates the mixture. When the solvent front has risen to about the length of the paper the strip is removed, the front marked in pencil and the strip dried.

blocks.long_description: A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line near the bottom of a paper strip, the strip is hung in a covered tank with its end dipping into solvent, and as the solvent climbs by capillary action each component travels at its own rate between the water held in the paper and the moving solvent, so the spots separate. The retardation factor is the distance a spot has moved divided by the distance the solvent front has moved, and it is fixed for a given substance and pair of phases, so matching Rf values against known samples identifies the components: in the printed chromatogram the mixture A contains B and C. Colourless spots are shown by ultraviolet light or a locating agent such as ninhydrin. One spot means a pure substance; purity is also judged by a sharp melting point, a sharp mixed melting point with a pure sample, or the boiling point for a liquid, as in the check of laboratory aspirin for unreacted salicylic acid.

blocks.prompt: On what basis are the components separated in paper chromatography, what are its phases, and why is water not generally used as the solvent (Quick Check 15.4a, b; exercise Q.2f, i, j)?
blocks.explanation: Components separate because each distributes differently between the stationary phase, the water held in the cellulose fibres, and the mobile phase, the organic solvent moving up the paper; those favouring the mobile phase travel farther. Water is not used as the mobile phase because it is the stationary phase; a mobile phase of water would not be immiscible with it and would carry everything together.

items: Paper chromatography (partition): stationary phase = water in the cellulose, mobile phase = organic solvent; ascending, descending or radial.
Ascending: covered tank, Whatman No. 1 strip, pencil line 2.5 cm, spots of sample and known compounds, dip 5 to 6 mm, components rise at different rates, mark the front, dry.
